query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles, the onset of premelting is governed by the preferential surface segregation and local melting of low‐melting Cu. This Cu-rich surface layer forms at sub‐bulk melting temperatures, lowering the effective melting onset and facilitating rapid atomic mixing during melting and subsequent rapid cooling.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid, compositionally homogeneous Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles with diameters of about 10–20 nm. A controlled baseline consists of otherwise similar nanoparticles made from a Cu-depleted (Fe–Ni–Cr–Co) alloy.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heating protocol using in-situ high-resolution imaging (e.g., in-situ TEM or neutron imaging) across the temperature range of 800–1300 °C, followed by rapid cooling to mimic high-temperature synthesis conditions.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted in an inert atmosphere with precisely calibrated temperature control (uncertainty ±15 °C) and identical thermal ramp rates for both HEA compositions. Nanoparticle sizes are uniformly maintained below ~30 nm to ensure dominant surface effects.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, Cu-enriched surface layer that transitions into a liquid-like phase at temperatures below the bulk melting point.
generation.mechanism: Upon heating, the higher mobility and lower melting point of Cu atoms drive their segregation to the nanoparticle surface. This results in a locally molten Cu-rich layer that initiates premelting at temperatures lower than the bulk melting point. The liquid layer then enhances atomic diffusion, promoting the re‐mixing and eventual consolidation of the solid solution during rapid cooling.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles will display an early onset of surface premelting (by approximately 15–30 °C lower than expected for the bulk alloy) as indicated by changes in surface morphology and compositional mapping. In contrast, the Cu-depleted baseline will show a higher and more uniform melting onset without significant surface premelting phenomena. During rapid cooling, the premelt-induced enhanced diffusion in the Cu-containing particles should result in improved homogeneity of the solid solution.
generation.baseline: Cu-depleted Fe–Ni–Cr–Co HEA nanoparticles that lack the low-melting Cu component and therefore are expected to exhibit a higher and less differentiated melting onset.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to nanoparticles with diameters below ~30 nm where surface effects are significant. It holds under inert atmospheres and controlled thermal profiles where oxidation is negligible. Larger particles, or those subjected to very slow cooling rates, may not exhibit the same pronounced premelting behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis extends previous in-situ imaging observations (PMC8320920::web::011) showing Cu-related melting onset and melting point depression effects observed in nanocrystalline simulations (PMC6479918::web::006) to the chemically complex HEA nanoparticle regime. Uncertainties remain regarding the exact temperature shift due to instrumental calibration and the impact of nanoparticle size distribution on the extent of surface segregation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one set of Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu HEA nanoparticles and one set of Cu-depleted Fe–Ni–Cr–Co HEA nanoparticles, both with similar size distributions (<30 nm). Using in-situ TEM (or neutron imaging), monitor the nanoparticles during a controlled heating ramp from 800 °C to 1300 °C to observe any early surface melting or formation of liquid-like surface layers. Follow this with rapid cooling. Post-experiment, use compositional mapping (e.g., EELS or EDX line scans) to detect surface segregation.
measurements: In-situ TEM or neutron imaging to capture morphological changes during heating
DSC to record the onset of premelting transitions
Surface-sensitive spectroscopy (EELS/EDX) for detecting Cu enrichment at nanoparticle surfaces
Comparative analysis of melting onset temperatures between the two systems
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-containing HEA nanoparticles do not show a distinct early formation of a Cu-rich liquid-like surface layer or if the onset temperature of premelting is not significantly lower (by ~15–30 °C) than that of the baseline Cu-depleted nanoparticles, then the hypothesis is falsified.
